doc.title: Pete Candoli interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 15, 1999

title: Studio playing, Hugo Friedhofer and writing for trumpet
summary: Pete explains how good composers write for trumpets, mentioning Friedhofer, Legrand and Roy Harris.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Do you have any recollections of days in the studio when you really were hurting for one reason or another? You really didn’t have it, and it was a struggle for you to get through a cue or something?

I don’t know. I really don’t know, because it’s a habit. You see when you’re considered a top studio player, your facilities, whatever it is, legitimately — you ever hear of “One Night Jacks” by Hugo Friedhofer, that’s a Marlon Brando picture?

What an orchestrator. I mean he is such a good composer that you don’t need a time, a clock to catch a cue. If you played naturally, like it’s written, it falls, that’s it. He’s just one of those people. And anybody that writes like this, they don’t use a C trumpet instead of a B flat trumpet, and write like it’s a B flat trumpet. There’s a difference in quality between the C. See it has a different edge, a different pitch. Good composers will know that and use it and write in the right register for that so it gets that sound. Things like this. Writing for, okay that’s a trumpet, it’s a trumpet. And these things become a matter of habit. The longer I was here, I’ve done so many of it, so many composers, like Michel, who’d rather sing and play piano instead of write. And he sounds terrible when he sings. I mean I love him, you know, but I remember he studied with Madame Boulanger, a French lady who used to teach composition and a lot of people have studied with her. But of all of the people who studied with her — Roy Harris, my composition teacher — he studied with her. He was a composer when he was 27. And good. And he says I’ve had some drawn out fights with her to prove her wrong. He says give me two weeks and I’ll assure you, you’re wrong, you know, musically that is. I mean there are some things that come out that are just unbelievable. And he said the person that showed Igor Stravinsky orchestration was a Frenchman, not the Russian that they say he studied with, no it was a Frenchman that taught him orchestration.
